records.title: Product Engineering Intern
records.summary: Worked across full-stack development and product development, translating requirements and functional needs into prototypes and product features from concept through to working software.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

Majara is a Saudi startup builder that turn business ideas into products and scalable businesses. I joined the team as a Product Engineering Intern, working hybrid out of Riyadh. Because the team is small and the work is closely tied to building new products, the role has been broader than a typical internship focused on a predefined engineering backlog.

My work has primarily involved building backend services and REST APIs in Python, connecting those services to frontend applications and external integrations, and prototyping new product capabilities from an initial requirement through to working software. The work often starts before there is a fully defined technical specification, which means part of the job is understanding the intended workflow, identifying what needs to exist technically, and then deciding how to structure and implement it.

A significant part of the role has been working directly with stakeholders to turn business needs into something an engineering team can actually build. I've participated in stakeholder discussions to understand the problem, clarify workflows, challenge ambiguous requirements, and translate those conversations into MVP definitions, functional requirements, user roles, and acceptance criteria. My previous experience in business development at SEET helped significantly here: I'm already comfortable speaking with clients, asking questions to uncover the underlying need, and translating business conversations into a concrete solution. At Majara, I've been able to apply that same skill from the engineering side — taking what a stakeholder needs and translating it into something that can actually be designed and built.

Once the requirements were defined, I worked on translating them into the technical structure behind the product: data models, API contracts, business logic, and system workflows. I then implemented and iterated on those capabilities as requirements became clearer through development. This exposed me to a part of product engineering that isn't visible in the final codebase: deciding what belongs in the MVP, identifying missing edge cases, and recognizing when a requirement needs to be clarified before it becomes an implementation problem.

The backend work has included Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery, Docker, and REST API design. I've also worked with external APIs and asynchronous workflows, which introduced practical engineering concerns around rate limits, retries, failures, and keeping the system predictable when dependencies don't behave perfectly.

I've also gained experience on the frontend side, working with React to connect product interfaces to the backend services I was building. This gave me a better understanding of the full path from user interaction to API request, business logic, database operation, and response back to the interface. Working across both sides also made it easier to spot gaps between what an API technically exposes and what the actual product experience requires.

Because the products are B2B, the users and constraints are different from those of a typical consumer application. The software needs to fit into an existing company's processes rather than simply provide a standalone feature. Multi-tenancy, access boundaries, predictable behavior, data integrity, and the ability to support different organizational workflows therefore become important parts of the design from the beginning.

Outside of my direct product work with Majara, I've also been deliberately developing my knowledge of AI engineering and LLM-based systems through personal projects and experimentation. That has included exploring tools such as LangChain and LangGraph and learning how retrieval, agent orchestration, and LLMs can be incorporated into software systems. These are currently areas I'm building toward rather than claiming as production AI experience.

What has made the experience particularly valuable is the exposure to the full path from **problem → stakeholder needs → MVP definition → requirements → architecture → implementation → iteration**. Rather than receiving a finished specification and only being responsible for the code, I've had to develop the ability to understand what is being asked, question gaps in the requirements, make engineering decisions, and turn an ambiguous idea into working software.

records.title: Business Development Intern
records.summary: Worked backward from client objectives to concrete proposals — client meetings, sales pitches, and ongoing relationships. It taught me to translate a loosely defined problem into a solution that's actually useful and deliverable, the same skill that scopes a good engineering requirement.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

Before Majara, I spent a few months in business development at SEET (صيت), a marketing solutions agency in Riyadh. The role was almost the inverse of engineering work: instead of starting with a technical requirement and figuring out how to implement it, I started with a client, their business objective, and often a loosely defined problem, then worked backward to determine what solution actually made sense.

The work was primarily client-facing and involved understanding what organizations were trying to achieve, identifying where SEET's services could create value, and turning those conversations into concrete proposals. Day to day, that meant participating in client meetings, understanding requirements and pain points, preparing sales pitches and proposal decks, presenting solutions, and staying involved in the relationship after the initial proposal rather than treating a signed deal as the end of the interaction.

A particularly useful part of the role was learning that clients rarely describe their problems in a way that maps neatly onto a service or solution. A client might come in with a broad objective, a business challenge, or simply an idea of what they think they need. The job was to ask the right questions, understand the underlying objective, and translate that ambiguity into a solution that was both useful to the client and realistically deliverable by the agency.

That translation happened at several levels: understanding the client's business problem, determining what SEET could realistically offer, communicating the value of that solution, and presenting it in a way that made sense to someone who wasn't necessarily interested in the underlying execution details.

The experience also taught me that business development isn't simply about selling. A large part of it is managing expectations and building enough understanding between two sides that the proposed solution actually matches the problem. A technically impressive solution that solves the wrong problem is still a bad solution, just as a persuasive pitch for something the client doesn't actually need is ultimately a bad outcome.

I think about this experience often on the engineering side now. A badly scoped technical requirement and a badly scoped sales pitch can fail for essentially the same reason: the person defining the solution didn't fully understand the problem. The skill that fixes both is the same one I developed at SEET — sit with the client or stakeholder, ask questions, challenge assumptions when necessary, and understand what they actually need rather than simply building around what they first asked for.

That experience is one of the reasons I don't see engineering and business development as completely separate skill sets. Engineering taught me how to build systems; SEET taught me to spend more time understanding **what should actually be built in the first place**.

records.title: Corporate hotel booking backend
records.summary: A FastAPI service that turns bulk employee trip requests into booked hotels — Amadeus search, bulk booking through Celery workers, and confirmation emails. I built the core flows solo: multi-tenant, idempotent, with retry and backoff around a rate-limited external API. Shelved before launch when industry regulations changed.
records.body:
## What the work actually involved

This was a backend proof of concept for a B2B corporate housing platform designed to solve a largely operational problem: companies often need to arrange accommodation for groups of employees, but the process can end up being handled manually by HR teams, project managers, or relocation staff. They may need to find suitable properties, negotiate with multiple suppliers, coordinate individual employee stays, track availability and costs, handle changes in headcount, and reconcile multiple bookings and invoices. As the number of employees grows, this becomes a time-consuming administrative job rather than something the company should have to manage manually.

The product was designed to centralize that process. Instead of a project manager coordinating dozens of accommodation arrangements separately, a company could manage its housing requirements through one platform, with bulk booking workflows, centralized booking information, and a single view of occupancy and accommodation costs. The broader business model was aimed at organizations such as consulting and contracting companies housing project teams, large HR departments managing relocation and housing, and recruitment companies arranging accommodation for incoming employees.

The backend I built was responsible for turning that product workflow into an actual system. I worked independently on the core FastAPI services, including REST APIs for hotel search, booking workflows, bulk operations, and related application logic. PostgreSQL stored tenant, traveler, and booking state, with SQLAlchemy providing the database layer and Alembic handling schema migrations.

A major part of the problem was connecting the platform to Amadeus for hotel availability and booking. The purpose of the integration was not simply to expose another API to users; it was to automate work that would otherwise require a person to search for and coordinate accommodation. That meant the integration had to be reliable enough to operate as part of a larger workflow.

Amadeus introduced constraints that shaped the architecture. Requests could be slow, rate-limited, or fail temporarily, and the application couldn't control those conditions. I therefore used Celery workers backed by Redis to process search and booking operations asynchronously where appropriate, keeping long-running external API work out of the main request/response cycle. The worker layer also provided a place to implement retries and exponential backoff rather than immediately failing a workflow when an external service experienced a transient problem.

Booking required an additional reliability guarantee: **retrying an operation could never accidentally create a duplicate booking**. For example, a request might time out after the external provider had actually processed it. Retrying blindly could then result in two reservations for the same traveler. I treated idempotency as a core requirement, using idempotency keys and designing the application-side write path so that repeating the same operation would not create duplicate bookings or duplicate state.

The system was also designed for multiple corporate customers sharing the same platform. Each company needed its travelers, requests, and bookings isolated from every other company, so tenant context was incorporated into the application and used to scope the relevant data. This allowed the platform to support a B2B SaaS-style model without requiring a separate deployment for every customer.

Bulk operations were particularly important because they mapped directly to the underlying business pain. The goal wasn't simply to make it easier to book one hotel room. It was to reduce the amount of repetitive coordination required when a company needed accommodation for an entire project team. That meant the system had to account for multiple operations happening together, including partial failures, retries, changes in employee requirements, and the possibility that some bookings succeeded while others did not.

The workflow could also trigger confirmation emails once bookings cleared the relevant process, keeping communication downstream from the booking operation rather than making email delivery part of the critical transaction.

The project ultimately did not reach production. It was shelved after changes in industry regulations affected the booking model the product was built around. That was a business and regulatory change rather than a technical failure.

What made the project valuable from an engineering perspective was the connection between the **business problem and the architecture**. The system wasn't complex simply because it used FastAPI, Celery, Redis, or PostgreSQL. Each major technical decision existed because of a real constraint: bulk workflows addressed the repetitive work handled by HR and project managers; asynchronous processing addressed slow and rate-limited external APIs; idempotency protected against duplicate bookings; and tenant isolation supported multiple corporate customers on the same platform.

The project gave me experience going beyond implementing isolated API endpoints and instead thinking about how a real business workflow should behave when it encounters unreliable dependencies, multiple users, changing requirements, and failure.

records.title: About
records.summary: Software engineer based in Riyadh, currently studying Information Systems in the Data Science and Management track and interning at Majara as a Product Engineering Intern. My work spans backend engineering, product development, and stakeholder-driven requirements, while I’m using this portfolio’s AI chat feature as a hands-on exercise in full-stack development, retrieval, and agent orchestration.
records.body:
## Who I am

I'm a software engineer based in Riyadh, currently studying Information Systems at King Saud University in the Data Science and Management track and interning at Majara as a Product Engineering Intern. My work sits at the intersection of software engineering and product development: understanding a problem, working with stakeholders to define what needs to be built, and turning those requirements into working software.

Before moving deeper into engineering, I spent a few months in business development at SEET (صيت), a Riyadh marketing agency. That experience shaped how I approach technical work today. It taught me to start with the question of what the other side actually needs rather than immediately jumping to a solution — a mindset I now apply when working with stakeholders and translating business problems into technical requirements.

Most of my hands-on engineering experience so far centers on backend systems: Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, REST API design, PostgreSQL, Redis, Celery, Docker, and pytest. I'm comfortable moving from a requirements conversation toward a working system, and I care about the parts of engineering that don't always show up in a demo — idempotency, retries, multi-tenancy, data integrity, and what happens when an external dependency misbehaves.

I'm also developing my skills across the rest of the stack. I've worked with React to connect frontend interfaces to backend services, giving me a better understanding of how decisions on one side of an application affect the other. More broadly, I'm interested in becoming the kind of engineer who can move between product requirements, frontend, backend, and infrastructure rather than being limited to a single layer of the system.

AI engineering is another area I'm actively exploring. I haven't built production AI products yet, but I've been deliberately learning how LLMs, retrieval, and agent-based systems fit into real software — this portfolio's chat feature is where that learning happens in practice. It's a deliberate exception to how I normally approach projects: where I'd usually default to the simplest tool that solves the problem, here I intentionally chose a more involved architecture — retrieval over this structured knowledge corpus, agent orchestration with LangGraph, and a self-hosted backend — specifically to get hands-on experience with the engineering challenges behind these systems, not to make the portfolio itself unnecessarily complex.

More broadly, I'm interested in the space where **software engineering, product thinking, and AI intersect**. I'm still early in my career, but I'm intentionally building toward roles where I can understand ambiguous problems, communicate with both technical and non-technical stakeholders, make sound engineering decisions, and turn those decisions into systems people can actually use.
